from: two decks of an algorithms course Folio wrote on 12 October 2026, after the writer was told to keep a function on one slide: slides by segment number

lesson1.title: Searching a list: linear and binary search
lesson1.notes: Welcome the class. Today students write linear search and binary search in Python, see why binary search needs a sorted list, and meet the final project. The course builds on last semester’s Python. Outline it in a few sentences: searching, sorting, how running time grows, recursion, and choosing an algorithm for a problem.

lesson1.title: How the course is graded
lesson1.notes: Put the table on screen and say what each component is. The quizzes are marked in points. The weekly problem sets and the final project are each student’s own work. Tell students they will meet the final project later in this session. Then ask each student to write down one question about the course and hear two or three.

lesson1.title: Guess my number: how many questions do you need?
bullets: Work from the sheet “Guess my number”.

lesson1.title: Linear search
lesson1.notes:
Describe linear search as the strategy of guessing in order from the guessing game: look at each item in turn and stop at a match or at the end of the list. It works on any list, sorted or not.

Before revealing anything, have every student write what the function should return when the target is not in the list, and why a plain 0 would be a poor choice. Hear two answers. Expected answer: -1, because 0 is a valid index. Mention once that Python’s `list.index` raises `ValueError` instead.

Then count comparisons for a list of 1,000,000 items. The worst case is 1,000,000.

lesson1.title: Write linear search
bullets: Work from the sheet “Write linear search”.

lesson1.title: The target is 61. Which half of the list can you now ignore, and what does low become?
lesson1.notes:
Link back to the guessing game: the best guess is the middle one. Explain low, high and mid, with mid = (low + high) // 2. Students predict on paper before anything is revealed.

Answer, for after they have predicted: mid is 7, which holds 42. Since 42 < 61, everything up to index 7 can be ignored, and low becomes 8.

lesson1.title: Binary search for 61 in a sorted list
lesson1.notes: Step through the demonstration one step at a time. The target 61 is found at index 10 after 4 comparisons (mid 7, 11, 9, 10). Linear search would need 11. Stress that mid has already been compared, so the next range excludes it.

lesson1.title: Your turn: write binary search
bullets: Write `binary_search(items, target)`. Return the index of the target, or -1 if it is not in the list.
lesson1.notes: Each student writes the function on paper, using the steps just shown. Do not project the code yet. Common slip to watch for: `low = mid` or `high = mid`, which can loop forever.

lesson1.title: Binary search in Python
lesson1.notes:
Students correct their own version and relate each line to a step of the demonstration. Stress `low = mid + 1` and `high = mid - 1`: mid has already been compared.

Compare the cost. A sorted list of 1,000,000 items needs at most about 20 comparisons, since 2²⁰ = 1,048,576. Linear search needs up to 1,000,000.

lesson1.title: Trace binary search on 16 numbers
bullets: Work from the sheet “Trace binary search on 16 numbers”.

lesson1.title: Why binary search fails on an unsorted list
bullets: Work from the sheet “Binary search on an unsorted list”.

lesson1.title: Find the bug and make up a case that shows it
bullets: Work from the sheet “Find the bug”.

lesson1.title: What is due, and what comes next
bullets: Weekly problem sets: due at the start of next time
Final project: deadline is on the project sheet
Practice quiz on today’s lesson: for after class
Optional reading: Bhargava, Grokking Algorithms (2016), ch. 1 (to confirm)
lesson1.notes:
Before students leave, set the weekly problem set, name it and say it is due at the start of next time. Do not describe its tasks. For the final project, point to the project sheet and say the deadline as it appears there.

Tell students that next time they sit a graded test, the in-class quiz, and that they will also code selection sort and insertion sort and count comparisons. The practice quiz on today’s lesson is for after class. The Bhargava chapter is optional further reading.

lesson2.title: Sorting by selection and insertion, and counting comparisons
lesson2.notes: Welcome students. Keep this brief and move to the plan for the session.

lesson2.title: Today’s plan
bullets: Today: selection sort and insertion sort, then an in-class quiz on searching and sorting
lesson2.notes:
Say that “Weekly problem sets: Searching a list: linear and binary search” is due now. It belongs to Weekly problem sets (40% of the course grade).

Tell students the in-class quiz comes later today, after the sorting work. It covers searching and sorting, is marked in points, and counts toward In-class quizzes (30% of the course grade). What students may bring or use will be announced just before the quiz begins.

Have the quiz papers ready, face down. Do not start on the sorting content here; the next part of the session begins it.

lesson2.title: Sort a hand by hand: what rule did you follow?
bullets: Work from the sheet “Sort a list by hand, then write your rule”.

lesson2.title: Predict the first pass
bullets: Prompt: after the first pass, what does 29, 10, 14, 37, 13 look like?
lesson2.notes:
Describe a pass first: scan the unsorted part for the smallest item, then swap it into the first unsorted place. Students predict on paper before you step through anything.

Answer for you: the smallest item is 10, at index 1. Swapping it with 29 gives [10, 29, 14, 37, 13].

lesson2.title: Selection sort, pass by pass
lesson2.notes:
Step through the demonstration with the list [29, 10, 14, 37, 13]. Students read the comparisons per pass off the demonstration, write them for 5 items and write the total. Then each writes the total for 8 items. Hear two answers.

For you: the passes make 4, 3, 2, 1 comparisons, 10 in all. For 8 items the total is 28. For 1,000 items it is 499,500. Selection sort always makes n(n−1)/2 comparisons, whatever the order of the input.

lesson2.title: Selection sort with a counter
lesson2.notes:
Show the whole function at once and relate each line to a step of a pass. The outer loop is the pass. `smallest = i` starts with the first unsorted place. The inner loop scans the rest. `count += 1` sits right before each comparison, so it counts comparisons only. The last line of the outer loop is the swap.

Common slip: counting swaps as comparisons. The swap is not a comparison, and it happens once per pass whatever the data.

lesson2.title: Insertion sort: sliding the key into place
lesson2.notes:
Explain with a hand of cards: the left part is in order, and the next item (the key) slides left past larger items until it fits.

Draw the insertion of key 2 on the board, counting comparisons as you go. Key 2 makes 1 comparison and gives [2, 5, 4, 6, 1, 3].

Students predict the list after key 4 is inserted. For you: key 4 makes 2 comparisons and gives [2, 4, 5, 6, 1, 3]. Students then finish the remaining insertions on paper, writing only the comparisons for each key and the total. Pairs compare totals for one minute, then hear the total.

For you: key 6 makes 1, key 1 makes 4, key 3 makes 4. The total is 12. Stress that the comparison that stops a slide still counts.

lesson2.title: Code insertion sort with a counter
bullets: Work from the sheet “Insertion sort with a counter”.

lesson2.title: Find the bug, then make up a list that shows it
bullets: Work from the sheet “Find the bug in a classmate’s insertion sort”.

lesson2.title: Same sorts, different inputs: does order matter?
bullets: Work from the sheet “Same sorts, different inputs”.

lesson2.title: Quiz
bullets: Quiz in progress. Work alone. Write your name at the top of the paper.
lesson2.notes:
Announce what students may bring or use. Ask them to clear their desks of everything else and to sit with a seat between neighbors where the room allows.

Students sit the paper alone and in silence, in the time given. Nothing about searching or sorting stays on the board or screen: wipe the board and show only the time left. Remind students at five minutes and at one minute. Anyone who finishes early waits quietly. At the end of the time the papers are collected.

lesson2.title: Problem set, next time and a last question
bullets: Work from the sheet “Last question: a list almost in order”.

lesson2.title: Due and next time
bullets: Weekly problem sets: due at the start of next time
Next time: merge sort by splitting, sorting, merging
Optional reading: Sedgewick and Wayne, Algorithms, 4th ed. (2011), section 2.1 (to confirm)
lesson2.notes:
Set the graded assignment under Weekly problem sets (40% of the course grade). It is each student’s own work, scored individually using the scoring on its sheet. Do not describe its tasks.

Next time students build merge sort by splitting a list, sorting the halves and merging them, then compare its comparison counts with these two sorts.

Say that a short practice quiz on today’s lesson is for after class and counts toward no grade. The reading is optional further reading.

Every student writes one line on the slip: which sort they would use on a list that is already almost in order, and why. Expected answer: insertion sort, because each key stops sliding almost at once, so the count is close to n−1. Hear two answers if time allows.
